passages.original: Subiodc ordina- tioni rhetor explicationem rerum commodare debebit. Quæ duabus partibus constat, structuræ qualitate et quantitate verborum. Hæc omnia memoria suscipit, quam et plerique Græcorum, et M. Tullius in primis oratori affirmat necessariam, hoc, ut opinor, modo : < Venio nunc ad thesaurum rerum omnium memo< riam ; quæ nisi custos inventis, ordinatisque rebus < athibeatur, intelligimus omnia, etiamsi præclaris< sima sint, in oratore peritura. i Memoriam pronuntiatio sequetur, res, ut Demostheni videtur, inter oratoria officia vcl prima vel sola: quæ consistit duo , uus , motu corporis et sono vocis. Hæc tantum summatim tetigisse satis est, quæ sunt oratoris officia. Re- liquum est viderc quid sit finis.
passages.english: Next, the rhetor will have to apply the expression of the matter to the arrangement. This consists of two parts: the quality of the composition and the quantity of the words. Memory takes up all these things, and many of the Greeks, and Marcus Tullius above all, declare it necessary to the orator, in this way, I think: "I come now to memory, the treasury of all things; unless it is applied as guardian to the things that have been invented and arranged, we understand that everything in the orator, however splendid it may be, will perish." Delivery will follow memory, a thing which, as it seems to Demosthenes, is either the first or the only one among the orator's duties; it consists of two [things], the movement of the body and the sound of the voice. It is enough to have touched briefly on these things, which are the duties of the orator. It remains to see what the end is.
passages.notes: Scanning errors corrected: 'Subiodc ordina- tioni' read as 'Subinde ordinationi'; 'athibeatur' as 'adhibeatur'; 'vcl' as 'vel'; 'viderc' as 'videre'. 'duo , uus' is garbled, probably 'duobus' (two [things]). The quotation is Cicero, De Oratore 1.18.

passages.original: Nee tam oportere spectari n:a- gnitudinem rerum ct personarum, quam rationem æqui et iniqui , veri ct falsi: eamdem enim esse horum in minimis vim, qu m in maximis. Talia principia sunt pluraque apud Demosthenem in iis libris qui inscribuntur Idiotici, et magis apud Lysiam , et apud quosdam ex nostris vcteribus. Cerle Marcus 'lullius cum pro Archia diceret, non alter exorsus est.
passages.english: [And it should be said that] one ought not to look so much at the greatness of the matters and persons as at the principle of fair and unfair, true and false; for these have the same force in the smallest matters as in the greatest. Such are the openings, and many of them, in Demosthenes in those books entitled Idiotici, and more so in Lysias, and in some of our own ancient [orators]. Certainly Marcus Tullius, when he spoke for Archias, began in no other way.
passages.notes: Scanning errors corrected: 'Nee' as 'Nec', 'n:a- gnitudinem' as 'magnitudinem', 'ct' as 'et', 'qu m' as 'quam', 'vcteribus' as 'veteribus', 'Cerle' as 'Certe', ''lullius' as 'Tullius'. The infinitive construction depends on the preceding 'dicat'. 'Idiotici' presumably refers to Demosthenes' private speeches (logoi idiōtikoi).
